weeks.theme: Plain Paper Validity & Stamp Duty Myth

tuesday.question: Can a Will be written on plain paper in India?
tuesday.content:
Under the Indian Succession Act, 1925, neither a lawyer nor stamp paper is legally mandatory to create a valid Last Will and Testament.

Here are the 3 statutory legal facts every Indian should know:

1. Plain White Paper is 100% Valid:
Under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, a Will is completely exempt from stamp duty across India. You can draft your Will on standard A4 paper.

2. Mandatory Legal Requirements (Section 63):
For your Will to be legally binding and court-admissible, you only need:
• The testator (you) must be of sound mind and sign/affix mark on the document.
• Two independent witnesses (above 18 years, who are NOT beneficiaries) must witness your signature and sign in your presence.

3. Registration is Optional:
Under Section 18 of the Registration Act, 1908, registering a Will at the Sub-Registrar's Office (SRO) is purely optional. An unregistered Will signed with 2 witnesses is legally valid.

If you want a properly structured legal draft aligned with Section 63 without paying ₹10,000–₹15,000 in lawyer fees, you can use automated legal platforms like SmartWill India (https://www.smartwillindia.in) to draft your court-valid Will in 10 minutes for ₹299.

weeks.theme: Nominee vs Legal Heir (Supreme Court Ruling)

tuesday.question: What is the difference between a nominee and a legal heir in Indian banks?
tuesday.content:
This is the single most dangerous financial misconception in India.

Many people think: "I made my elder son the nominee for my ₹50 Lakh FD, so the money belongs to him."

Under Indian Law, this is FALSE.

1. What the Supreme Court Ruled:
In landmark judgments (Sarbati Devi v. Usha Devi and Shakti Yezdani v. Jayanand Jayant Salgaonkar), the Supreme Court ruled that a NOMINEE is merely a 'custodian' or 'trustee' of the funds — NOT the legal owner.

2. The Nominee's Actual Legal Role:
The nominee is just a recipient authorized by the bank to collect the payout on the deceased's behalf. Once collected, that money must be distributed to ALL legal heirs according to succession law (or according to a valid Will).

3. The Only Solution:
If you want your nominee to also be the exclusive owner of your assets, you MUST specify this explicitly in a legally valid Will.

Without a Will, your legal heirs can take the nominee to civil court for their rightful share.

tuesday.question: Can an NRI make a Will for property in India without travelling to India?
tuesday.content:
Yes, absolutely. Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act 1925, an NRI residing anywhere in the world (USA, Canada, UK, UAE, Australia, etc.) can execute a legally valid Will for their assets in India without travelling to India.

Key Legal Rules for NRIs:

1. The 'Lex Situs' Rule:
Under Private International Law and Section 5 of the Indian Succession Act, succession to immovable property (flats, plots, agricultural land) in India is strictly governed by the law of India — NOT foreign law.

2. Foreign Wills Cause Probate Nightmares:
If you only execute a Will in California or Ontario, your heirs in India will need an 'Ancillary Probate' in an Indian court, which can take 18–36 months and cost ₹2L–₹5L in lawyer fees.

3. How to Execute an India-Specific Will Abroad:
• Draft an India-specific Will covering your Indian properties and NRE/NRO accounts.
• Print it on plain A4 paper.
• Sign it in front of 2 independent witnesses overseas (colleagues or friends over 18 who are not beneficiaries).
• Registration at the Sub-Registrar Office in India is purely optional (Section 18, Registration Act).

Here is what happens behind the scenes:

1. Immediate Account Freeze:
Once the bank receives information of the depositor's demise, all debit transactions, NetBanking, and ATM cards are immediately frozen to prevent fraud.

2. The ₹40,000 Crore Reality:
According to official RBI data, over ₹40,000 Crore currently lies unclaimed in Indian bank accounts (transferred to the DEA Fund). The primary reason? Inability of grieving families to produce legal succession proof.

4. How a Will Solves This Instantly:

tuesday.question: How are mutual funds and shares inherited in India?
tuesday.content:
With millions of Indians investing in Zerodha, Groww, AngelOne, and mutual fund platforms, inheriting digital wealth has become a critical topic.

Here is how demat assets and mutual funds are handled after death:

1. SEBI Transmission Norms:
SEBI has standardized the transmission procedure. If a single nominee exists, the shares/units are transmitted to the nominee upon submitting the death certificate and KYC.

2. But Beware of Legal Heir Claims:
Just like bank accounts, SEBI nomination does NOT extinguish the rights of legal heirs. If a brother or sister claims their legal share under personal law, the nominee cannot retain 100% of the portfolio unless protected by a Will.

3. Mutual Fund Folios with Different Nominees:
If you have folios across multiple AMCs (HDFC, SBI, Nippon) with different or outdated nominees, your family will face endless paperwork.

4. The Best Practice:

tuesday.question: Is it mandatory to register a Will in India?
tuesday.content:
No, it is 100% optional.

Under Section 18(e) of the Registration Act, 1908, the registration of a Last Will and Testament is expressly OPTIONAL throughout India.

Here is what Indian courts have established:

1. Legal Validity of Unregistered Wills:
The Supreme Court of India has held in multiple judgments that an unregistered Will has the exact same legal sanctity in a court of law as a registered Will, provided the requirements of Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act 1925 are satisfied:
• The testator signed of sound mind without coercion.
• Two independent witnesses attested in the testator's presence.

2. Why Do People Register Wills?
Registration merely creates a public record at the Sub-Registrar's Office (SRO) and provides additional proof of execution. However, registration does NOT grant immunity from challenge.

3. The Cost Reality:
Lawyers often charge ₹15,000–₹25,000 claiming registration is compulsory. Don't be misled.

tuesday.question: Do married daughters have equal rights in father's property in India?
tuesday.content:
This is governed by the landmark 2020 Supreme Court ruling in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma.

Here is the legal reality regarding daughters and fathers' property:

1. Ancestral Property (Coparcenary):
Under the 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act, daughters have an equal coparcenary birthright in ancestral property, regardless of whether they are married or whether the father was alive in 2005.

2. Self-Acquired Property (Crucial Distinction):
If the property is self-acquired (bought with the father's own earnings, salary, or investments), the father has 100% absolute freedom to bequeath it to ANYONE through a valid Will.
• He can leave 100% to his daughter.
• He can leave 100% to his wife or son.
• He can even leave it to a charitable trust.

3. What if There is NO Will?
If the father dies without a Will, his self-acquired property is divided EQUALLY among all Class-I heirs (wife, mother, sons, and daughters).

tuesday.question: Who can be a witness to a Will in India?
tuesday.content:
Choosing the wrong witnesses is the #1 mistake that causes Wills to be contested or invalidated in Indian courts.

Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, here are the non-negotiable rules for witnesses:

1. Two Witnesses are Mandatory:
A Will must be attested by a minimum of TWO witnesses.

2. Who CANNOT be a Witness (Fatal Mistake):
• A beneficiary (someone inheriting property in the Will) should NEVER sign as a witness. Under Section 67, any bequest made to an attesting witness is completely VOID.
• The spouse of a beneficiary should also avoid witnessing to eliminate claims of conflict of interest.

3. Who SHOULD be a Witness:
• Independent individuals over 18 years of sound mind.
• Ideal choices: A family physician/doctor (who can certify sound mental health), long-time family friends, neighbors, or colleagues.

4. How Attestation Works:
Both witnesses must see the testator sign, and both witnesses must sign in the physical presence of the testator.
